doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

chapter: Open City and the economics of records
title: Streaming, free music and records as calling cards
summary: Davis says recordings no longer recoup costs and serve as calling cards, yet big bands keep multiplying in New York.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Is there — with technology these days — is there a feeling sometimes that you’re giving it away for free?

For sure, yeah. It is very challenging and if I were doing a project like “Open City” like I said for the money or in the hopes of recouping the investment in it, it would be foolhardy. There is, you know the old time go down to Tower Records and spend $8 or $10 on a record and that’s it and you know, people can make bootleg cassettes or whatever. But now I mean pretty much as soon as the record comes out it’s on YouTube for free. So you know I think there are people who — I’m certainly one of them — that when I — I want to buy the music because I want to support the artist that I’m getting so much joy and enjoyment out of listening to. So to me I think there are a lot of people like that but then I think there are a lot of people that — especially in the younger generation, in fairness to them, you know they’re used to getting everything for free in terms of their music, or at a very low cost. So these streaming services like Apple or Spotify, whatever, the amount, it’s fractions of a penny every time it gets played. So there’s little hope of making much other than pocket change back from that side of things. You know I have my own company, Hip-Bone Music and so we’ll sell the arrangements through that so that’s a possible revenue stream in terms of recouping. It still won’t get anywhere near your initial investment. But I think you look at it in the sense that it’s an expensive

calling card. Or business card. It’s saying here’s my new stuff that I’ve been working on and hopefully the byproduct is some gigs you weren’t expecting maybe or appearances at a college or a high school that wants to hire you as a guest, those type of things. And I do think that that is a lane that you can get in and have some success with that. But again you’re still — you have to make an initial investment that probably won’t be recouped.
Musicians are going to do it anyway, aren’t they?

Absolutely. Absolutely. Yeah I mean it’s actually quite amazing to me how many big bands are going right now in New York over the last couple years. Big band leaders, younger players all the way up to folks my age and ten, fifteen years older than me. Yeah. I mean they keep coming, they keep doing it, and it’s great. It’s great. Because that’s what it is — it is about the music and it is about serving the music and getting it out there. So I think it’s great that people are passionate about their music and their projects and it’s important. But you’re right, the musicians are going to keep doing that regardless of the shortfall in terms of the economics.
